route: Washington National to Fort Lauderdale, via Tampa
outcome: 74 of the 79 people on board and 4 people on the bridge died
summary: Heavy snow had closed Washington National Airport for a while, and the flight left about 1 hour 45 minutes late. The airplane was de-iced, then waited a long time in falling snow before its takeoff clearance. The engine anti-ice was not switched on, so ice on the engine sensors made the thrust gauges read higher than the real thrust.

During the takeoff run the first officer said several times that something did not look right, but the takeoff continued. With snow and ice on the wings, the 737 pitched up and could barely climb. Less than a mile past the end of the runway it hit the northbound span of the 14th Street Bridge, striking cars, and went into the ice-covered Potomac River. Four passengers and one crew member survived.
cause: The NTSB found the probable cause was the crew's failure to use engine anti-ice during ground operation and takeoff, their decision to take off with snow and ice on the wings, and the captain's failure to reject the takeoff when his attention was called to the unusual engine readings. Contributing were the long wait between de-icing and takeoff, the 737's known tendency to pitch up with even small amounts of contamination on the wing leading edge, and the crew's limited experience of jet winter operations.

lines.speaker: Washington tower
lines.text: Taxi into position and hold... be ready for an immediate [takeoff].

lessons: The accident became a standard lesson in winter operations: the time between de-icing and takeoff matters, and a crew that sees snow or ice on the wings should not take off.
It showed how ice on an engine's pressure sensor can make the thrust gauges read wrong, and why engine anti-ice must be on when the conditions call for it.
The first officer pointed out the abnormal engine readings several times during the takeoff run. The NTSB included the captain's failure to reject the takeoff in the probable cause.
pathNote: Straight lines between the start and end of runway 36 (FAA data via OurAirports; the runway is numbered 1/19 today) and the crash site at the 14th Street Bridge (Wikidata), which is 0.79 nautical miles from the runway end. The report gives 0.75.

keyPoints.text: Engines spool up on runway 36 with 74 passengers and 5 crew on board.

keyPoints.label: End of runway
keyPoints.text: Witnesses said the airplane lifted off well down the runway and climbed slowly, nose high.

keyPoints.label: 14th Street Bridge
keyPoints.text: Hits the northbound span and goes into the Potomac River, 0.75 nautical miles from the end of the runway.

outcome: One flight attendant was lost; 94 people survived
summary: As the 737 leveled off at 24,000 feet on a short interisland flight, about 18 feet of the cabin roof and upper walls behind the entrance door tore away. A flight attendant standing in the aisle was swept out of the airplane. Seven passengers and another flight attendant were seriously injured.

The captain took control, made an emergency descent and diverted to Kahului on Maui. The left engine stopped during the approach because its control cables had been damaged. The crew landed on runway 02 about 13 minutes after the failure. After the accident, a passenger said she had seen a crack in the fuselage while boarding at Hilo, but did not mention it to anyone.
cause: The NTSB found that Aloha Airlines' maintenance program failed to find significant disbonding and fatigue damage, which led to the failure of a lap joint and the separation of the upper fuselage. Cracks had started at many rivet holes along the joint at once. Contributing were weak supervision of maintenance, weak FAA oversight, an FAA directive that did not require inspection of all the lap joints Boeing had proposed, and the lack of a complete fix for early 737 lap joint bonding problems.

lines.speaker: The first officer, to Maui tower
lines.text: We're going to need assistance. We cannot communicate with the flight attendants. We'll need assistance for the passengers when we land.

lines.speaker: The first officer, to Maui tower
lines.text: We won't have a nose gear.

lines.speaker: The crew, to Maui tower
lines.text: We'll need all the equipment you've got.

lessons: The airplane had cracked in many places along one joint at the same time, known as multiple site damage. The NTSB asked that new airliners be fatigue tested to at least twice their planned service life, and that manufacturers find structure prone to multiple site damage and set inspections for it (A-89-67).

Interisland flights are very short, so Aloha's airplanes flew far more pressurisation cycles per flight hour than maintenance programs assumed. The NTSB asked the FAA to identify such operators and make sure their maintenance catches cycle related damage (A-89-54).

The report found inspectors missed cracks that were there to be found. The NTSB asked for formal certification and recurrent training of inspectors who do nondestructive testing (A-89-56), and for better FAA oversight of airline maintenance programs.

keyPoints.label: Landing at Kahului
keyPoints.text: Lands on runway 02 with one engine. Everyone left on board is evacuated on the runway.

route: Denver Stapleton to Philadelphia, with a stop in Chicago
outcome: 111 of the 296 people on board died; 185 survived
summary: In cruise at 37,000 feet, the fan disk in the tail-mounted engine broke apart. Fragments cut the lines of all three hydraulic systems, so the pilots lost their normal flight controls.

The crew, joined by a United check pilot who was travelling as a passenger, steered by changing the thrust of the two wing engines. They flew to Sioux City and touched down on a closed runway, 22, about 44 minutes after the failure. The right wing hit the ground first, and the airplane broke up and caught fire. 185 people survived.
cause: The NTSB found the probable cause was that United's engine overhaul inspection did not find a fatigue crack in the stage 1 fan disk, which started from a defect made when the disk was manufactured. When the disk came apart, the debris went beyond what the hydraulic system design was protected against.

lines.speaker: Sioux City approach (as the report describes it)
lines.text: Reports the airplane 21 miles north of the airport and asks for a wider turn, to keep it away from the city.

lines.speaker: The captain
lines.text: Whatever you do, keep us away from the city.

lessons: The NTSB asked for redundant "second set of eyes" inspections of critical engine parts such as fan disks (A-90-167, A-90-176, A-90-177).

It asked the FAA to review how flight control power sources are protected and made redundant on current airplanes, and to encourage backup flight control systems on new wide-body designs (A-90-168, A-90-169).
An infant held on a parent's lap died. The NTSB had already recommended that young children be restrained in a seat suited to their height and weight (A-90-78).

After that the line joins two positions the report gives as distances from Sioux City ("about 35 miles northeast" and "21 miles north", placed as nautical miles because air traffic control uses them) and the crash site from Wikidata. The real track included several right turns that are not drawn.

route: New York JFK to Paris Charles de Gaulle
summary: About 12 minutes after takeoff from JFK, while climbing over the Atlantic south of Long Island, the 747 broke up in flight and fell into the ocean about 8 miles south of East Moriches, New York.

Investigators recovered the wreckage from the sea floor and rebuilt part of the airplane. They found that the centre wing fuel tank, which held only about 50 gallons of fuel, had exploded. Heat from equipment under the tank had warmed the fuel vapour inside, making it flammable.
cause: The NTSB found the probable cause was an explosion of the centre wing fuel tank, from ignition of the flammable fuel and air mixture in it. The ignition source could not be determined with certainty; the most likely was a short circuit outside the tank that let too much voltage into it through the wiring of the fuel quantity indication system.
lessons: Until then, certification assumed fuel tank explosions could be prevented by keeping ignition sources out. The NTSB said that was not enough and asked for ways to stop tanks from holding explosive fuel vapour at all, giving "significant consideration" to nitrogen inerting systems (A-96-174).
It asked the FAA to review how wiring for safety critical systems is separated, and to fix the ignition risk from silver sulfide deposits on fuel quantity parts inside tanks (A-00-106, A-00-107).
It pushed for better care of ageing wiring: maintenance training, reporting of unsafe wiring, and new technology such as arc fault circuit breakers (A-00-108).
pathNote: The dashed line is only a straight join between JFK runway 22R and the accident site; the airplane actually left to the southwest and turned east along the coast. The accident site is the centre of the main wreckage area whose corner coordinates are given in the NTSB report.

keyPoints.label: Takeoff
keyPoints.text: Leaves JFK runway 22R for Paris, more than an hour late, with 212 passengers and 18 crew.

keyPoints.label: Accident site
keyPoints.text: The recorders stop as the airplane breaks up. The main wreckage lies on the ocean floor about 8 miles south of East Moriches.

route: Paris Charles de Gaulle to New York JFK (charter)
timeZone: UTC (local time was two hours later)
outcome: All 109 people on board and 4 people on the ground died
summary: Late in the takeoff run, just after V1, a tyre on the left main landing gear ran over a strip of metal that had fallen from an airplane that took off five minutes earlier. The tyre burst, and pieces of it struck the underside of the wing.

A fuel tank was ruptured and the leaking fuel caught fire. Two engines lost thrust and the landing gear would not retract. The crew tried to reach Le Bourget airport, but the airplane crashed onto a hotel in Gonesse about a minute and a half after the tyre burst.
cause: The BEA found the causes were the high-speed passage of a tyre over a part lost by an aircraft that had taken off five minutes earlier, the ripping out of a large piece of fuel tank by energy from a tyre fragment, and ignition of the leaking fuel, causing a very large fire and severe loss of thrust on engines 2 and 1. The landing gear that could not retract probably helped keep the flame burning.

lines.speaker: Charles de Gaulle tower
lines.text: ... 45 90 you have flames ... you have flames behind you.

lines.speaker: Charles de Gaulle tower
lines.text: 45 90 you have strong flames behind you ... as you wish you have priority for a return to the field.

lessons: Before Concorde flew again, the authorities required flexible linings in six of its fuel tanks, stronger electrical wiring in the landing gear bays, and new Michelin NZG tyres.
The BEA recommended stronger certification requirements for aircraft tyres, and certification rules that take account of fuel tank damage from debris and the ignition of fuel leaks.
It also recommended regulations on inspecting runways for debris, since the strip of metal was lying on the runway.
pathNote: The takeoff run follows runway 26R (runway data from OurAirports; the report gives its length as 4,215 metres). The metal strip is placed in the middle of the 1,642 to 1,845 metres the BEA gives. After the runway, the line goes straight to the crash site in Gonesse (Wikidata), 9.6 km from the threshold; the BEA says about 9,500 metres. The real flight path curved left.

keyPoints.label: Tyre burst

keyPoints.label: End of runway

keyPoints.text: Crashes onto a hotel at La Patte d'Oie in Gonesse, at the junction of the N17 and D902 roads.

summary: Over the Atlantic at night, a fuel line on the right engine cracked and began leaking. A week earlier, during an engine change, a newer style hydraulic pump and fuel tube had been fitted next to an older hydraulic tube that did not match them, and the two tubes rubbed together.

The crew saw a fuel imbalance about an hour after the leak started, but did not recognise it as a leak. They opened the crossfeed to balance the tanks, which sent fuel from the good left tanks to the leak, and diverted to Lajes in the Azores. Both engines stopped from fuel exhaustion, the second one 65 nautical miles out at about 34,500 feet. The crew glided for about 19 minutes and landed on runway 33. During the evacuation 2 people were seriously hurt and 16 had minor injuries.
cause: Portugal's investigators found that a mismatched hydraulic tube and fuel tube, installed during the engine change, rubbed together and cracked the fuel tube. The crew did not identify the leak and carried out the fuel imbalance procedure from memory, which fed fuel from the left tanks to the leak. Not running the FUEL LEAK procedure was the key factor that led to fuel exhaustion.
lessons: Airbus added a FUEL FU/FOB DISCREPANCY alert to the A330. It warns the crew when the fuel on board plus the fuel used differs from the takeoff fuel by more than 3,500 kg (Service Bulletin A330-28-3080, 2002).

France's DGAC made a revised A330 FUEL LEAK procedure mandatory (Airworthiness Directive 2002-548(B)). Transport Canada told crews about the signs of a fuel leak (CBAAC 190), and Air Transat added fuel leak scenarios to its simulator training.
Within days, Airbus and Rolls-Royce had every A330 with Trent 700 engines checked for clearance between the fuel and hydraulic lines.

On the maintenance side, the report found the engine change relied on verbal advice instead of the service bulletin that described the correct parts, and called for better planning of major component changes.
pathNote: From 04:08 on, the line joins the positions in the report's flight data table. The dashed part before that is only a straight line from Toronto to the oceanic entry point 45N 50W; the planned route went by Halifax. Airport positions are from Wikidata.

keyPoints.label: Leak starts

keyPoints.label: Imbalance noticed
keyPoints.text: The crew sees a fuel imbalance advisory. About 12.3 tons of fuel are left.

keyPoints.label: Crossfeed opened
keyPoints.text: Fuel from the left tanks starts feeding across, and into the leak. At 05:45 the crew starts the diversion to Lajes.

keyPoints.label: Right engine stops
keyPoints.text: Flame out at 39,000 feet, about 150 miles from Lajes.

keyPoints.label: Left engine stops
keyPoints.text: Both engines are out at about 34,500 feet, 65 nautical miles from Lajes. The glide begins.

keyPoints.label: Landing at Lajes
keyPoints.text: After a 360 degree turn and S-turns to lose height, crosses the runway 33 threshold at about 200 knots and stops 7,600 feet down the runway.

summary: About two minutes after takeoff from LaGuardia, the A320 flew into a flock of Canada geese at about 2,800 feet above the ground. Birds went into both engines and the airplane lost almost all of its thrust.

The crew judged that they could not reach LaGuardia or Teterboro, turned south along the Hudson River and ditched the airplane on the water near the ferry terminal in Weehawken, New Jersey. The 150 passengers and 5 crew got out onto the wings and slide rafts, and ferries and rescue boats picked them up within minutes.
cause: The NTSB found the probable cause was the ingestion of large birds into each engine, which caused an almost total loss of thrust in both engines.

quote.text: Hit birds, we've lost thrust in both engines, we're turning back towards LaGuardia.
quote.speaker: The captain, to the LaGuardia departure controller

lines.speaker: The captain, asked if he wants runway 13 at LaGuardia
lines.text: We're unable. We may end up in the Hudson.

lines.speaker: The captain
lines.text: I'm not sure we can make any runway. Uh what's over to our right anything in New Jersey maybe Teterboro?

lines.speaker: The captain, asked which Teterboro runway he wants
lines.text: We're gonna be in the Hudson.

recording.label: New York TRACON, LaGuardia departure position (FAA release, February 2009)
recording.note: The full 20 minute recording from the controller's position (20:20 to 20:40 UTC), including quiet gaps. The player starts at 7:20, just before the captain's first call about the birds at 15:27:33 local time. The FAA page is gone, so this plays the copy kept by the Internet Archive.

lessons: The Airbus dual engine failure checklist the crew used was written for a failure above 20,000 feet. The NTSB asked the FAA to require a checklist for a dual engine failure at low altitude (A-10-66) and to add that scenario to pilot simulator training (A-10-69).

Engine bird ingestion certification tests were questioned. The NTSB asked for the flocking bird tests to be reviewed, including whether large birds hitting the engine core should be tested (A-10-64, A-10-65).

Crews had little training for ditching. The NTSB asked for ditching guidance and training for pilots, and for new airplanes to show that their ditching conditions can be reached without engine power (A-10-70, A-10-72).

The NTSB asked that every certificated airport assess its wildlife strike hazard (A-10-75). It also credited the crew's teamwork and decision making, the cabin crew's fast evacuation and the nearby ferries for everyone surviving.

outcome: All 49 people on board and 1 person on the ground died
summary: On a night approach to Buffalo in light icing, the airplane slowed as the crew lowered the landing gear and flaps. The stick shaker warned of an approaching stall.

The captain pulled back on the controls instead of lowering the nose, and the airplane stalled. The stick pusher activated three times, but the crew did not recover. The airplane crashed into a house in Clarence Center, about 5 nautical miles northeast of the airport.
cause: The NTSB found the probable cause was the captain's inappropriate response to the stick shaker, which led to a stall from which the airplane did not recover. Contributing were the crew's failure to monitor airspeed against the rising low speed cue, not following sterile cockpit rules, the captain's failure to manage the flight, and Colgan's inadequate procedures for airspeed selection in icing conditions.
lessons: The NTSB asked for stall training that includes fully developed and unexpected stalls, and stick pusher training in the simulator (A-10-22, A-10-23).
It asked airlines to manage fatigue risks from pilots commuting to work (A-10-16), and asked for complete pilot training records that new employers can see (A-10-17 to A-10-20).

The accident led to the Airline Safety and Federal Aviation Administration Extension Act of 2010, which raised the experience required to be an airline first officer and required the FAA to update its pilot rest rules.
pathNote: The dashed line is only a straight join between Newark and the crash site in Clarence Center (Wikidata). The report gives no positions for the route.

keyPoints.label: Clarence Center

route: Rio de Janeiro Galeão to Paris Charles de Gaulle
timeZone: UTC; the flight left Rio on the evening of 31 May
summary: The A330 was cruising at 35,000 feet over the Atlantic at night, in the clouds of the intertropical convergence zone. The captain had gone to rest and the two copilots were flying. Ice crystals most likely blocked the pitot probes, and for about a minute the airspeed readings were wrong. The autopilot and autothrust disconnected and the flight controls changed to alternate law.

The pilot flying made large roll inputs and pulled the nose up. The airplane climbed to about 38,000 feet, lost speed and stalled. The stall warning sounded, but the crew never recognised the stall and did not apply a recovery. The airplane descended in the stall for about three and a half minutes and hit the sea at 02:14:28. The wreckage was found almost two years later, 3,900 metres down.
cause: France's BEA found a chain of events: a temporary inconsistency in the airspeed readings, likely from ice crystals blocking the pitot probes; control inputs that destabilised the flight path; the crew not linking the loss of airspeed to the right procedure; and the crew not identifying the approach to the stall or the stall itself, so no recovery was made.

quote.speaker: The pilot not flying, 11 seconds after the autopilot disconnected

lessons: The BEA made 41 safety recommendations covering flight recorders, certification, pilot training, relief of the captain, search and rescue, air traffic control, simulators, cockpit design and oversight.

It recommended that EASA make specific and regular training mandatory for manual handling of the approach to stall and stall recovery, including at high altitude. The report noted the copilots had not been trained for this.

Finding the recorders took almost two years. The BEA recommended extending underwater locator beacons to 90 days and studied triggered transmission of flight data, so an airplane in trouble sends its data before it is lost.
It asked EASA and the FAA to evaluate requiring an angle of attack indicator that pilots can see directly, since nothing else showed the stall clearly.
pathNote: The dashed part from Rio to INTOL is only a straight line; the real route followed the Brazilian coast. From INTOL the line joins the route waypoints named in the BEA report (INTOL, SALPU, ORARO), the last position the airplane sent, and the wreckage site. Waypoint positions are from published navigation data (OpenNav).

keyPoints.label: Takeoff

keyPoints.label: INTOL

keyPoints.label: SALPU

keyPoints.label: Last position sent

keyPoints.label: Wreckage site

sources.name: BEA final report on AF 447 (English translation, FAA copy)

outcome: 3 of the 307 people on board died
summary: On a clear day, with the glideslope out of service, the crew flew a visual approach to runway 28L. The airplane was high, and in trying to get down the pilot flying selected an autopilot mode that started a climb. He disconnected the autopilot and pulled the thrust levers to idle, which put the autothrottle in a mode where it no longer controlled airspeed. Nobody noticed.

The airplane came down below the glidepath and the airspeed fell well below the target. The crew started a go-around too late. The main landing gear and tail hit the seawall short of the runway, and the airplane slid and spun on the runway before stopping. Three passengers died.
cause: The NTSB found the probable cause was the crew's mismanagement of the descent during the visual approach, the pilot flying's unintended deactivation of automatic airspeed control, the crew's inadequate monitoring of airspeed, and their delayed go-around. Contributing were complex autothrottle and autopilot systems that were not well described in Boeing's documentation and Asiana's training, nonstandard crew communication, inadequate visual approach training, inadequate supervision by the instructor pilot, and fatigue.
lessons: The NTSB asked for better Boeing 777 training on autothrottle modes, including when the autothrottle does not protect against low speed (A-14-37 to A-14-40).
It asked for an expert review of how crews are trained to understand automation, and a design review of how the 777 controls airspeed (A-14-41, A-14-42).
It asked for design requirements for low energy alerting systems that warn a crew when speed and height are running out (A-14-43).
pathNote: The dashed line across the Pacific is only a straight join from Incheon. The approach is drawn along the runway 28L centreline using distances from the NTSB report: final approach joined about 14 nm out, 5 nm, the seawall 600 feet before the displaced threshold, and the stop about 2,400 feet from the seawall. Runway positions are from OurAirports.

keyPoints.label: Departure
keyPoints.text: Leaves Incheon for San Francisco with 291 passengers and 16 crew. The flight crosses the date line and 8 time zones.

keyPoints.label: 14 nm final
keyPoints.text: Joins the final approach course about 14 nautical miles out, slightly above the 3 degree glidepath.

keyPoints.label: 5 nm
keyPoints.text: After keeping 180 knots to 5 nm as asked by air traffic control, the airplane is well above the glidepath.

keyPoints.label: Seawall
keyPoints.text: The stick shaker activated at 11:27:46 and the go-around call came at 11:27:47.8. The landing gear and tail strike the seawall.

keyPoints.label: Stop
keyPoints.text: After spinning about 330 degrees, the airplane stops off the left side of the runway, about 2,400 feet from the seawall.
